summary: Two range towers on Castle Neck at the Ipswich River mouth, lit 1837; front light dropped 1932, and the 1881 rear tower went to Edgartown in 1939.

light.lamps: fixed white; multiple oil lamps and reflectors, originally ten in each tower

structures.status: standing; shows a white light every 4 seconds

corrections.why: USLHS place records print 1809 for both towers, but Congress appropriated the money in 1837 and the New England Lighthouses and Lighthouse Friends histories put the first lighting on 1 December 1837. No source read supports 1809.
The 1881 cast-iron rear tower was moved to Edgartown in 1939 to replace a damaged lighthouse; it was relocated, not lost.
The steel tower built in 1939 on the rear site is described in 2024 as emitting a white light every 4 seconds; the front light was discontinued in 1932 (see resolved_conflicts).

corrections.proposed: add {role: rear_range, type: steel skeleton tower, material: steel, built: 1939, status: standing}
corrections.why: The 1939 steel skeleton tower erected on the site is not in the record.
Historic Ipswich says the Coast Guard took over the light and serviced it after 1939.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS disposition gives 'Two Towers Est. 1838', while the New England Lighthouses and Lighthouse Friends histories put the towers and the first light in 1837. The story gives 1837 for the lighting and says the towers were put up in 1837-38.

USLHS gives 1809 for both records; Rowlett gives 1837 (record events); New England Lighthouses and Lighthouse Friends give 1 December 1837 with the Notice to Mariners of 13 November 1837. Taken as 1837.

Wikidata lists both active and inactive. The front light was discontinued in 1932 (USLHS, New England Lighthouses), but Historic Ipswich in 2024 describes the steel tower on the rear site as emitting a white light every 4 seconds. Treated as active.

New England Lighthouses and Lighthouse Friends date the 45-foot cast-iron rear tower to 1881; the USLHS disposition note and Ellsworth's own journal (as Historic Ipswich prints it) say 1880. The story gives both and does not settle it.

The USLHS roster and Lighthouse Friends give Ellsworth 1861 to 1902 and Greenwood in three stints; Historic Ipswich's keeper list gives Greenwood 1838 to 1852 without a break and Ellsworth from 1852, while its own text gives 1861 for the appointment. The story states the disagreement.

resolved_conflicts.field: Deposit rescue of the captain's wife
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Ipswich Register as reprinted (1839) has the wife lowered from the stern on ropes; New England Lighthouses and Historic Ipswich say the men persuaded her to jump from the rigging. The story gives the newspaper version and states the later variant.

notes_for_editor: (1) Deposit wreck date: the Newport Rhode-Island Republican (1 Jan 1840) says the wreck came on a Sunday night, the 15th of the month (OCR 'Sunday wight, 15th iust'; check the page image at the loc.gov URL in source 7). The Ipswich Register report, as reprinted, has Marshall finding the wreck on a Monday morning and is quoted from a Friday issue, which must be 20 December or earlier; that points to 15/16 December. The New England Lighthouses, Lighthouse Friends and Historic Ipswich all give 23 December, which the paper evidence does not support. The story states both and does not settle it. (2) Garibaldi (Proctor, quoted in Historic Ipswich): 'Tuesday, March 11th, 1872' is internally wrong (11 March 1872 was a Monday). Historic Ipswich also dates Ellsworth's medal to 1873; Lighthouse Friends dates a rescue to March 1874. Not reconciled. (3) Rear tower height: the record's 6.0 m is not supported by New England Lighthouses or Lighthouse Friends, which both give 45 feet (13.7 m) for the 1881 cast-iron tower; the Wikipedia lead infobox gives 6 m for a tower and was not cited. Left unchanged in the record; a human should check the Coast Guard Light List or a survey. (4) New England Lighthouses dates the Thomas H. Lawrence grounding to September 1839; its own 'centennial of the Deposit' phrase and Historic Ipswich both point to 1939. (5) Source 2 roster matched by name and position (0.31 km); lines copied exactly as printed. Caretaker lines use the USLHS heading 'Watchman / Caretaker' and are coded 'other'. (6) The 1809 date in the USLHS records has no supporting source among those read; proposed correction in corrections. (7) The Coast Guard Historian's Ipswich Light page could not be read: the archived captures return only the Wayback index, so it is not cited. (8) Wikipedia was read for leads only. (9) Lighthouse Board reports for 1837-1890 are not in the local corpus; the 1837-1861 construction and keeper facts rest on Lighthouse Friends, New England Lighthouses and Historic Ipswich, and should be checked against the 1838-1880 Light-House Board reports if they can be reached. (10) Printed page numbers for the Light-House Board scan pages 57 and 87 were not read; cited as scan pages. (11) Historic Ipswich reprints a family memoir of the Lane caretakers; only the caretakers' roster names and the NEL statement about Crane Estate pay are used, and no personal family details. (12) The sources do not say whether the front beacon survives, who owns the ground now, or whether the grounds are open to visitors; access and visit fields left empty. (13) No photos added: the Commons images in the record have no confirmed licence. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28 (independent checker): (a) Quote check passed on first run (0 missing). (b) The 1895 Life-Saving Service entry ('Stranded on the bar outside Ipswich Harbor, 4 miles from station') is verbatim on scan p.160 (printed p.155 per OCR head); the OCR does not show which station the row belongs to, and the page image could not be fetched (the IIIF host returned 502). The story does not name the station; check the image before naming one. (c) The Ellsworth journal entry 'In 1880 a new lighthouse was built of iron' is quoted via Historic Ipswich; the journal itself was not read. (d) Historic Ipswich's 'A Complete List of the Keepers' gives 1838-1852 and 1852-1902 and is cited for the disagreement. (e) The Lawrence wreck is from a family recollection printed on Historic Ipswich; the story calls it a recollection. (f) The story states that 'Lighthouse Friends says' and 'Historic Ipswich says' for every contested fact; the Proctor quotation is second-hand via Historic Ipswich. (g) The 'Monday ... 16 December or earlier' argument follows from the Register's Friday issue as printed in the 25 December Boston reprint; the 16 December date is an inference and is labelled as one. (h) Units: 550 feet now carries 168 m; thirty feet carries 9.1 m. (i) Living people: no keeper after 1942 is named beyond the USLHS roster lines already in the research record.
